prompt.context: Your client is a consumer electronics retail chain selling products such as TVs, DVD players, digital cameras, and cell phones. Sales have varied dramatically across your client's stores with several experiencing a severe decline in revenues over the past two years.
prompt.question: How can you help the client even out performance across the individual stores and increase performance of the entire chain through organizational change?

clarifying_info.q: Is the sales decline happening across all stores or only some?
clarifying_info.a: Only a limited number of stores are experiencing the severe decline.

clarifying_info.q: Is this a revenue problem, a cost problem, or both?
clarifying_info.a: The primary issue is a decline in revenues at certain stores.

clarifying_info.q: Are competitors performing better in the same markets?
clarifying_info.a: Treat external factors as a possible branch to explore, but the focus should be on internal issues.

exhibits.title: Product Sales and Margin Data (Single Declining Store)
exhibits.shows: A table showing 5 product lines with their 2007 sales, gross profit in dollars, gross profit margin %, sales for 2005/2006/2007, and 2-year CAGR.

framework: Separate external factors (competition, market demand shifts) from internal factors
Internal: Product mix selection and shelf placement
Internal: Sales force knowledge and training quality
Identify which product lines are declining and why; correlate with margin and product complexity

questions.prompt: Design an issue tree or hypothesis tree to diagnose the sales decline.
questions.guidance: Level 1 should separate externalities (competition, demand decline) from internal issues. Candidate should be steered to internal issues. Internal branches should include marketing, product mix, employee knowledge/training, incentive programs, and customer service.

questions.prompt: Using the data provided, calculate the 2-year Sales CAGR for each product line.
questions.guidance: Candidate should know or be given the CAGR formula. Correct application and interpretation of results is the key skill here. Declining lines (Accessories, Digital Cameras, Video Camcorders) are the ones with highest margins and greatest product complexity.

steps: Accessories: (1.40/2.50)^0.5 - 1 = 0.749^0.5 - 1 = 0.866 - 1 = -13.4% (casebook rounds to -25%; note: casebook likely uses a different base or rounded figures — casebook-stated answer is -25%)
math.answer: Accessories: -25% (casebook figure); Plasma TV: +5%; DVD Player: +5%; Digital Cameras: -10%; Video Camcorders: -20%

questions.prompt: What pattern do you see in the data, and what does it suggest about the root cause?
questions.guidance: The product lines with negative CAGRs (Accessories, Digital Cameras, Video Camcorders) are those with the highest gross profit margins (50%, 30%, 40%). These are also the most technologically complex products requiring higher customer knowledge. Growing lines (Plasma TV, DVD Player) have lower margins (20%, 15%) and are more commoditized. The root cause hypothesis: customers buying high-complexity, high-margin products need knowledgeable sales associates to guide purchase decisions; poor training leads to lost sales precisely in these categories.

questions.prompt: What is the organizational issue driving poor training, and how is it perpetuating the problem?
questions.guidance: Training is currently decentralized through an apprenticeship model. In poorly performing stores, poor associates train new associates, perpetuating low quality. There is no consistent baseline of product knowledge across the chain. This structural weakness hits hardest on products that require active sales assistance.

brainstorming.prompt: What solutions would you recommend to fix the training and organizational issues and improve performance across all stores?

categories.name: Centralized Training
ideas: Establish centralized training seminars at corporate headquarters
Store managers attend HQ training and cascade knowledge back to staff
Distribute standardized training materials to all stores
Create product knowledge certification requirements for associates

categories.name: Manufacturer Partnerships
ideas: Negotiate with product manufacturers to provide in-store collateral and brochures
Share training costs with manufacturers through trade spend negotiations
Invite manufacturer reps for in-store product demonstrations

categories.name: Incentive Structure Reform
ideas: Introduce quantitative productivity metrics such as Sales per Average Hour (SPAH)
Link compensation or bonuses to high-margin product sales
Tie incentive payouts to completion of training certifications

categories.name: Performance Management
ideas: Identify and share best practices from high-performing stores
Set minimum performance benchmarks per store
Use mystery shoppers or customer satisfaction scores to monitor associate quality

recommendation: Centralize the sales associate training program: conduct seminars at HQ for store managers, who then train their staff using standardized materials, eliminating the apprenticeship model that perpetuates poor performance in weak stores
Prioritize training depth on high-margin, high-complexity categories (Accessories, Digital Cameras, Video Camcorders) where the revenue loss is greatest
Adjust the incentive structure to reward associates for high-margin product sales and training completion, using metrics like SPAH to track productivity
risks: Centralized training requires upfront investment in curriculum development and logistics
Store managers may resist culture change away from the apprenticeship model
Margin improvement may lag as training takes time to show results in sales
next_steps: Pilot the centralized training program in 2-3 low-performing stores and measure CAGR improvement over one sales cycle
Negotiate trade spend agreements with key manufacturers (camera, camcorder brands) to subsidize training collateral costs
Define SPAH targets per product category and integrate into store manager scorecards
